title: Error Correcting Code
body:
Noticing that a message arrived wrong is [[Error Detection]]. **Repairing it without asking for
a retransmission is error correction**, and it is the same idea one rung further: send more bits
than the message needs, chosen so that the legal messages sit far apart from each other.

That is the whole trick. There is nothing clever in the received bits themselves; the cleverness
is in having decided in advance which bit patterns count as legal.

## Redundancy and distance

A **code** is a chosen subset of all possible bit strings. The chosen strings are **codewords**;
everything else is illegal and therefore evidence of an error.

The **Hamming distance** between two strings is the number of positions where they differ. The
**minimum distance** $d$ of a code is the smallest distance between any two of its codewords, and
it alone decides what the code can do:

| Minimum distance | What it buys |
|---|---|
| $d \ge 2$ | detect 1 error |
| $d \ge 3$ | detect 2, **or correct 1** |
| $d \ge 5$ | correct 2 |
| general | detect $d - 1$, correct $\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor$ |

The correction rule is nearest-neighbour decoding: assume the fewest errors happened, and snap the
received string to the closest codeword. Correcting $t$ errors needs $2t + 1$ distance, because the
balls of radius $t$ around two codewords have to stay disjoint. Detecting only needs the received
string to miss every codeword, which is why detection is always cheaper than correction.

**The price is bandwidth.** A code sending $n$ bits per $k$ bits of message has *rate* $k/n$, and
every scheme below is a point on the trade between rate and $d$.

## Parity, the $d = 2$ code

One extra bit making the total number of 1s even. $d = 2$: any single flipped bit makes the count
odd, and there is no way to tell which bit it was. This is the 68000's bus parity in
[[Error Detection]], and it is a **linear equation over $GF(2)$**:

$$p = b_1 \oplus b_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus b_k$$

Addition mod 2 is XOR, so the check is "do all the bits XOR to zero". Two flipped bits cancel and
the code sees nothing, which is exactly what $d = 2$ predicts.

## Hamming codes, the $d = 3$ code

Use several parity bits, each covering a different overlapping subset of the message bits. The
Hamming(7,4) code sends 4 message bits and 3 parity bits:

```
positions   1  2  3  4  5  6  7
            p1 p2 m1 p3 m2 m3 m4

p1 checks positions 1,3,5,7   (bit 0 of the index set)
p2 checks positions 2,3,6,7   (bit 1)
p3 checks positions 4,5,6,7   (bit 2)
```

Recompute all three parities on receipt. The three pass/fail answers, read as a binary number, are
the **index of the broken bit**, and zero means nothing broke. Flip that bit and the message is
recovered. The overlapping-subset design is the whole point: each parity check halves the search,
so 3 checks locate 1 error among 7 positions.

This is [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] over a two-element field. The parity checks are the rows of a matrix
$H$, the codewords are exactly the vectors with $Hx = 0$ (the null space), and the syndrome $Hx$
of a corrupted vector names the error. Any code built this way is a **linear code**, and the
whole design problem is choosing $H$.

## Reed-Solomon, the code in everything

Hamming fixes single bits. Real damage is not single bits: a scratch on a disc, a coffee stain on
a QR code, and a dead drive in an array all destroy a **contiguous run**. Reed-Solomon fixes
whole symbols, and a symbol is a [[Byte]].

Treat $k$ message bytes as the coefficients of a degree-$(k-1)$ polynomial over $GF(2^8)$, then
transmit its **values** at $n$ fixed points instead of its coefficients:

```
message  m₀ m₁ … m_{k-1}   →   f(x) = m₀ + m₁x + … + m_{k-1}x^{k-1}
transmit f(a₁), f(a₂), …, f(a_n)          n > k
```

Any $k$ of those values pin the polynomial down uniquely, because two distinct degree-$(k-1)$
polynomials agree in at most $k-1$ places ([[Polynomial Ring]]). So the extra $n - k$ values are
pure redundancy, and **any $n - k$ lost symbols can be reconstructed** by interpolating from the
survivors. Corrupted symbols (position unknown) cost twice as much as erased ones (position
known), which is why RAID and CD players go out of their way to know *where* the damage is.

It needs a [[Finite Field]] rather than ordinary arithmetic for one reason: the argument requires
dividing by non-zero elements, and $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$ has zero divisors while $GF(2^8)$ does not.
Every non-zero byte is invertible there, so the interpolation always goes through.

## Where it actually runs

| Place | Code |
|---|---|
| CD, DVD, Blu-ray | Reed-Solomon, interleaved so a scratch spreads across many codewords |
| QR codes | Reed-Solomon, four selectable rates up to ~30% recoverable |
| RAID 6, erasure-coded object storage | Reed-Solomon over the drives, drives-as-symbols |
| ECC DRAM | Hamming-style SECDED: single error correct, double error detect |
| Deep space probes | heavy codes, because retransmission is hours away and may be impossible |
| Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G | LDPC and turbo codes, iterative decoding, near the theoretical limit |

**Interleaving** is the trick that makes bit-level codes survive burst damage: scatter each
codeword's symbols across the medium so that one physical burst puts a single symbol into each
of many codewords, and each one is then a correctable single error.

## The three-rung ladder

This note is the middle rung of a story the vault tells across three folders:

| Rung | Where | What it owns |
|---|---|---|
| detect | [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]], [[Error Detection]] | parity on the 68000 bus: the error is noticed, not repaired |
| **correct** | `Books/`, this note | Hamming and Reed-Solomon: recover the bits |
| the algebra | [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]], [[Finite Field]] | why arithmetic on bytes is a field, and where codewords come from |

There is a fourth reading in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]]. Decoding a *random* linear code is
NP-hard, so [[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] runs the whole construction backwards: McEliece hides a
structured code inside a scrambled-looking one and uses "decode this" as the hard problem. The
same polynomials [[AES]] uses for confusion are used here for repair, and there for hardness.

## Core facts

- Detection needs $d \ge 2$; correction of $t$ errors needs $d \ge 2t + 1$.
- Correction is always more expensive than detection at the same error count.
- A parity bit is one linear equation over $GF(2)$, and XOR is its addition.
- Hamming(7,4) locates a single-bit error because the failing checks spell out its index.
- Linear code = null space of a parity-check matrix $H$; the **syndrome** $Hx$ identifies the error.
- Reed-Solomon works on symbols (bytes), not bits, which is what makes it survive bursts.
- An erasure (position known) costs one symbol of redundancy; an error (position unknown) costs two.
- Interleaving converts a burst into many single-symbol errors.
- Retransmission is the alternative to correction, and it is the better answer whenever the round
  trip is cheap. ECC exists for the cases where it is not.
